articles.title: Public good and spaces
articles.content: NINETY-FOUR per cent of youth had no access to a library, 93pc to a sports facility, and 78pc to a park. Ninety-seven per cent had never been to a live music event, 94pc to a sports event, and 97pc to the cinema. A whopping 71pc had no access to any of the above. These figures are from a survey conducted for UNDP’s Pakistan National Human Development Report 2017: Unleashing the potential of a young Pakistan, of which Dr Adil Najam and I were the lead authors. It was a national survey that highlighted a youth population with few opportunities for positive engagement outside their home. Since 2017, the economy has not been doing well. We have not had any significant positive changes in national human development outcomes, and the impact of Covid and global slowdown has hardly been encouraging. So, one would expect that since conditions have not changed much, a similar survey carried out today would show numbers that are not very different from those reported then. I have been staying in London for the last couple of months. There is a large park about 400 metres away from our place. The park is managed by the local council (local government). It has a walking/ jogging track running along its almost kilometre-long perimeter. The park has two multipurpose fields. I saw them being used as cricket fields in August and they were converted into football and rugby fields in September. There are three hard-surface tennis courts on one side. There is a children’s play area with lots of structures to climb, swing from, and slide on. The play area is full most evenings. The park is utilised well. Hundreds of children, parents, and dogs visit it every day. Walkers, dog-walkers — most of whom pick up their pet’s poop themselves — and joggers are there round the clock. The tennis courts, play area, and fields get busy in the afternoon after school on weekdays. They are occupied throughout the day on weekends. Every afternoon, four to five groups of young people, with their coaches, have training sessions in the park. There are always cricket or football matches going on. On weekends, quite a few groups have picnics there too. The park is, of course, open to all. We have not had any significant positive changes in national human development outcomes. It would not be an overstatement to say that the park defines the neighbourhood and its vibe. It is a very family-oriented area and one sees that parents are comfortable allowing their young children to run around the park or ride their bike or scooters around the jogging track — often unsupervised. A lot of credit for this goes to the local council. The park does require significant upkeep for cleaning and maintaining the track, trees and plants, and the grassy fields. But, since residents can benefit from healthy activities, the council provides the needed services quite diligently. Walking down our area’s high street takes us to the local public library, which is also run by the local council. Since we are a family of readers, and buying books is not cheap, we went in to check if we could be members of the local library. All it took was proof of residence in the area to obtain membership cards free of cost. We then had access to not just the local library but all public libraries around the council (six, I think). One person can borrow up to 20 books at a time for up to three weeks. If a book is not available at our library, we can request it from other libraries in the network that have it. Over the last two weeks, my daughter has read six to seven books. Imagine the saving! And she has had fun learning and managing her own library membership card as well as the activity of borrowing and returning books. I am a little worried that the speed at which she is going, she might not have much left to read at the library in a month or two! Providing access to books is just a small part of the services on offer. The library has very inviting spaces for sitting and reading, and even desks for writing. It has free Wi-Fi and free access to internet-connected desktops for members. It also has at-cost facilities for printing and photocopying, and a decently priced cafeteria. There are also some rooms and spaces that can be booked for group activities. I have seen language-learning, meditation, and book-discussion clubs using these spaces. It has been a bit of a surprise to see a broad cross-section of society using these facilities. The book section for the young is always bustling. And from teenagers to retirees, all age groups are well represented throughout the day at the library. The local council provides all these public spaces. Local accountability for local issues seems to work well here. It is difficult to list all the benefits that accrue to the citizens from these two spaces and the free services that come with them. There are opportunities for physical, mental, and emotional engagement through group activities, social interaction, reading and learning, and hobbies and interests. It is important for all people to have such opportunities for these healthy activities, so that they can interact positively and learn to work together, and, generally, become engaged citizens. The contrast between where we need to be and the findings of the survey of Pakistani youth mentioned earlier could not be starker. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
articles.author: Faisal Bari

articles.title: Animal rights in Pakistan
articles.content: FOR almost as long as Pakistan has existed, the state has had one answer to stray dogs: kill them. Poison and bullets have been the tools, and rabies control the justification. Yet after decades of culling, dogs still roam our streets, bite cases keep coming, and children still die of a disease that is entirely preventable. That contradiction is now being argued in court, and the arguments are producing something larger than a verdict on dogs. Over the past two years, our courts have begun to treat the welfare of animals as a constitutional question. Pakistan may be witnessing the birth of a new branch of law. There is a precedent for this. Environmental law in Pakistan was shaped less by legislation than by judges, who recognised that the right to life under Article 9 means more than bare survival and includes the right to a healthy environment. Driven in large part by the work of Dr Parvez Hassan in the Shehla Zia case, that jurisprudence turned ecology into a matter of fundamental rights. Animal law is now following the same path, and for similar reasons. The World Health Organisation is clear that dog-mediated rabies is eliminated by vaccinating dogs, not by killing them. Mass vaccination, combined with humane population control through trap-neuter-vaccinate-return (TNVR), breaks the chain of transmission. Culling does not: it leaves gaps that unvaccinated dogs quickly fill, so the population and the disease both bounce back. Punjab recognised as much when it adopted an Animal Birth Control (TNVR) Policy. The trouble is that municipal authorities kept on culling anyway. Animal law is not simply about preventing cruelty, but also about public health, biodiversity and good governance. That gap between policy and practice is what brought Eiraj Hassan vs Government of Punjab, which one of us filed, to the Lahore High Court. The petition secured interim protection against illegal culling across the province, followed by directions that the policy be implemented in letter and spirit. The argument was taken further in Nelofar vs Chief Commissioner ICT, where principles of humane population management and animal sentience were developed. Read alongside the Islamabad High Court’s recognition of animal sentience in the Kaavan case, these rulings form an emerging body of law that treats animals as living beings whose welfare is bound with the health of society, not as property or pests. The constitutional basis is not hard to find. Articles 9, 9A and 14 protect life and dignity, and our courts have long held that environmental degradation and threats to public health can violate both. Animal welfare belongs in the same frame. Wildlife trafficking, inhumane food systems, badly managed animal populations and the spread of zoonotic disease all bear directly on human health. The global public health community calls this ‘One Health’: the well-being of people, animals and the environment cannot be separated. The pandemic taught that lesson at enormous cost. There is also a public safety argument. Decades of criminological research show that cruelty to animals frequently coexists with domestic violence, child abuse, and other violent crime. Violence against the powerless rarely stays confined to one kind of victim. A legal system that takes animal cruelty seriously is better placed to protect vulnerable people too. Animal rights do not compete with human rights; they reinforce them. Dogs are only the beginning. Public interest petitions have since been filed over illegally imported monkeys, lions kept in circuses and private zoos, endangered black bears used for entertainment, the condition of farm animals, regulation of animal carts, and the enforcement of slaughter laws, where better practice serves both animal welfare and the containment of zoonotic disease. Each case makes the same point in a different setting: animal law is not simply about preventing cruelty, but also about public health, biodiversity, and good governance. The groundwork outside the courtroom matters as much. In January 2025, Pakistan’s first International Animal and Environmental Rights Conference brought more than 700 judges, lawyers, academics and activists together with international organisations working in the field. It treated animal law not as a matter of charity but as a serious legal discipline. Kinnaird College in Lahore now teaches courses on animal rights law and food legal systems, and a new generation of lawyers is taking up this work. But courts can only go so far. Judgements set principles; governments must turn them into practice. Punjab, which already has the right policy on paper, should fund TNVR programmes properly, train municipal staff, and hold officials accountable when culling continues in defiance of court orders. Other provinces and the federal capital should follow. Legislators should look again at a cruelty law that dates back to 1890 and at the patchy regulation of zoos, circuses and the wildlife trade. Universities and bar associations should keep building the expertise that litigation alone cannot supply. If that happens, the past two years may be remembered not merely as a run of important cases, but as the moment Pakistan’s legal system began to take animals seriously. Environmental law changed how we understand our relationship with nature. Animal law can do the same for our relationship with the creatures we share it with. A society that protects its most vulnerable living beings is, in the end, a more just society for everyone in it. Altamush Saeed is a lawyer who holds an LLM in animal law & environmental law and teaches animal law and food law at Kinnaird College, Lahore. Eiraj Hassan is a social media manager for the PSL at the Pakistan Cricket Board.
articles.author: Altamush Saeed | Eiraj Hassan

articles.title: ‘Thinking’ Islam
articles.content: IT is a common belief that ‘religion is a matter of blind faith’. Often, Iqbal’s famous verse is quoted to support this view which says, “Be khatar kood pada aatish-i-namrud mein ishq/ Aql hai mahw-i-tamasha-i-lab-i-baam abhi”. The gist: love leapt fearlessly into Nimrod’s fire; while reason stood numb at the edge watching the spectacle. On the contrary, it is the same Iqbal who says, “Jahan-i taza ki afkar-i-taza se hai numud/ Ki sang-o-khisht se hote nahin jahan paida” (New worlds are [created and] driven from fresh thoughts; [remember] new worlds are not brought to life from [dead] stones or wood). Iqbal alludes here to the necessity of fresh thinking and innovative ideas that help create new worlds. What we argue for is a thinking Islam that promotes not only faith, but equally the intellectual search to explore the signs, symbols, metaphors (aayaat) of God, spread out both through the Word of God (the Book) and the Work of God (all around us) as speaking verses. While the Quran — and perhaps all sacred literature — makes humans surrender to the awe and wonder of the Supreme Being, their intellects are invited to explore the signs, symbols, metaphors, and stories (qasas) that are often narrated in simple, but highly sophisticated language. Many Quranic verses promote thinking and reflection. One fascinating verse is: “Many are the jinn and men we have made (zara’na) for Hell: they have hearts wherewith they understand not, eyes wherewith they see not, and ears wherewith they hear not. They are like cattle — nay more misguided: for they are heedless” (7:179). Reinforcing this, another verse says, “Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like cattle; nay, they are even farther astray from the Path” (25:44). Still another verse making a poignant point is: “Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Or are there locks upon their hearts?” (47:24). These and many other similar verses may be seen as strong counsel to promote thinking, reflection, and contemplation regarding God’s signs (aayaat). Using human sources of knowledge — the senses, and the heart (the seat of contemplation) — to explore God’s creation becomes a critical duty of humans. Commenting on these verses, Hussain Nasr et al in The Study Quran (2015) argue, “… the cattle do not possess an intellect with which to understand religious truth. Those who do not employ their intellect are thus no better than beasts — in fact, they are even worse for squandering the gift of intellect”. Interestingly, if we reflect on the verse, we come to realise that God does not mention any other aspect of faith so consequential (destined to hell) except not thinking and not using one’s senses. The verses imply that if these are not used, humans could be destined for perdition. These verses are supplementary to another set of verses in meaning and purpose, such as “Do they not look at the camels, how they are made? And at the sky, how it is raised high? And at the mountains, how they are fixed firm? And at the Earth, how it is spread out?” (88:17-20). Those who do not reflect are referred to by the Quran as heedless. “Or do you think that most of them listen or understand? They are only like cattle — no, more than that, they are astray from the Right Way!” (25:44). These are powerful reminders of Divine power and we need to reflect upon them. The Holy Book further says: “Had we but listened or used our intelligence we should not (now) be among the Companions of the Blazing Fire!” (67:10); “Will they then not meditate on the Quran, or are there locks on the hearts?” (47:24). Yet another verse of the Quran beautifully sums up what is being argued here, ie, God’s message about thinking and using our sources of knowledge to explore Allah’s creation. It says, “Lo! In the creation of the heavens and the earth and (in) the difference of night and day are tokens (of His Sovereignty) for men of understanding. Such as remembering Allah, standing, sitting, and reclining, and consider the creation of the heavens and the earth, (and say): Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain. Glory be to Thee! ...” (3:190-191). It is here in this verse that the Divine twin purpose for humans — remembering God and reflecting (on His creation) — comes out clearly. This connects both ritual and reflection fused together in a way that arouses our imagination to see them as compatible, and complementary, reinforcing each other. In sum, despite these clear imperatives of reflection, would one still insist that religion is only belief and has nothing to do with thinking? Our thinkers, curriculum writers, and ulema should highlight this dimension in their daily teaching and preaching. The writer is an educationist with an interest in the study of religion and philosophy.
articles.author: Jan-e-Alam Khaki

articles.title: Let them eat cake
articles.content: YET another World Bank report has been publishedhighlightingthe unending immiseration of Pakistan’s working people. Pakistan’s economic plight is described as largely on par with war-torn countries in the Arab region like Syria and Yemen. Unsurprisingly, the bank makes only limited mention of its own role in relentlessly enforcing the ‘structural adjustment’ policies which have greatly contributed to mass impoverishment. But the report is damning nonetheless. Almost 20 per cent of Pakistan’s 260 million people now fall into the extreme-poor category, defined as a daily income of less than $3. Extreme poverty has increased three-fold in less than a decade. If the poverty line is simulated at the slightly higher daily income level of $4.20, almost half of Pakistan’s people are poor. It is not all doom and gloom, of course, because Pakistani capitalists, landlords, and state mafias are doing very well. This is reflected in inequality markers. What economists call the Gini coefficient is at its highest level in almost 40 years. The report goes on to name a series of ‘shocks’ which have triggered the huge uptick in poverty; the Covid pandemic and the 2022 floods top the list. Missing is a meaningful political economy analysis in which class exploitation, colonial statecraft, and aid dependency are accorded the centrality that our sordid experience demands. In a nutshell, Pakistan’s masses are the targets of a scandalous class war that becomes more intense with each passing day. The main protagonists of this war are Pakistan’s own militarised ruling class and its external patrons, including the World Bank, IMF and bilateral ‘partners’. Even where the World Bank report notes that rising poverty and inequality is partly the result of a “prolonged period of economic adjustment that weakened real household incomes and employment opportunities”, the mention of the actual players that push the adjustment agenda is conspicuous by its absence. And there is nothing about Pakistan’s own state mafias, capitalists and landed magnates who happily pass on spiralling debt burdens to the people, whilst profiting endlessly through real estate and trade, with no concern for livelihoods and ecologies. Working families are eating less on the whole. There have been donor reports, which go beyond superficially describing social crises and actually name some names. In 2020, the UNDP’s annual Pakistan National Human Development Report explicitly stated that Pakistan’s militarised ruling class benefits from hidden — and sometimes overt — subsidies to the tune of $17.4 billion per annum. Six years later, one can assume that this figure has grown; it is another matter that donors are seemingly unwilling to name the protagonists of this class war as explicitly now as in 2020. The truth deficit extends to our own political classes and intelligentsia. Yes, one could argue that ‘elite capture’ has become a widely used phrase. Petrol bombs and other markers of inflation come in for regular criticism and parties like the Jamaat-i-Islami are given licence to undertake sanitised protests. But the political and intellectual mainstream is least concerned with the banality of everyday class war in comparison to intra-elite palace intrigues and diplomatic ‘successes’ in the geopolitical realm. Indeed, mainstream political conflict in Pakistan features only shades of the right, and the object of politics is to secure the good graces of the establishment, which in turn continues to rely on the age-old policy of securing geostrategic rents from external patrons. It is thus that the mass of Pakistan’s people has been thrust further down the class ladder for at least a decade, and arguably longer. Throughout this period, the actual political-economic order has remained largely unchanged, irrespective of who has occupied the formal seat of government. The accumulation of crises has made the present moment particularly desperate. The ruling regime proclaims its macroeconomic achievements while promising that the windfalls of its great accomplishments abroad will materialise soon. But the statistics that they do not advertise tell the real story. Working families are eating less on the whole and even less nutritiously than before; kids are pulled out of school and forced to work to supplement meagre household incomes; even those who imagine themselves as white-collar workers, let alone those who are in the category of extreme poor, contemplate killing themselves and their offspring to preserve their dignity. It is thus that one is reminded of the 18th-century ‘French princess’ to whom the reply ‘let them eat cake’ was attributed, when her advisers explained that the mass of her subjects were not able to afford bread. The French Revolution followed some years later. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
articles.author: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar

articles.title: Beneath the surface
articles.content: THE IMF’sstaff-level agreementwith Pakistan on the fourth balance-of-payments and the third climate financing reviews came with little drama — which itself says something. The mission spent two weeks in Islamabad, wrapped up the 2026 Article IV consultation, and left with a deal that releases $1.2bn once the IMF Executive Board approves it. Nobody expected a different outcome. The Fund is unlikely to push hard against a borrower that is hitting its fiscal targets. Compare this withMarch, when talks went virtual, ended without an agreement, and dragged on until the Board cleared funds in May. The recent round made fewer headlines because the hard bargaining over the budget had already been done. The current budget is built around a primary surplus of 2pc of GDP, and the lender is now collecting on that commitment. A programme that has settled into a routine reassures markets. It also shows how little room Islamabad has to depart from the script. The lender’s own assessment is generous. It says the authorities have successfully navigated the fallout of the Middle East conflict and that policies have preserved stability. Reserves stand at about $21.5bn and inflation has eased from its May peak. Yet, a closer look shows that, at 10.3pc in September, inflation remains well above the State Bank’s medium-term target range. Last year’s growth of 3.6pc, with an annual population growth of nearly 2pc, leaves per capita gains thin. The World Bank put poverty at about 42.4pc for 2025, and said growth was too weak to prevent an additional 1.9m people from slipping below the line in a single year. Exports tell the same story. Goods exports fell about 6pc to $30.1bn, of which textiles accounted for $17.9bn. Imports rose 8pc to $69.8bn, widening the merchandise trade deficit to $39.6bn. Growth in IT services kept total exports near $40bn, which though welcome, is no substitute for a manufacturing base that sells more abroad. The recommendations deserve more attention than the headline figure. The lender wants thefuel support schemephased out, calling it costly and too broadly targeted. Unwinding a broad subsidy is politically harder than agreeing to end it on paper. It also wants timely tariff adjustments so that the circular debt does not return, a medium-term tax strategy, private participation in power distribution, better governance of SOEs, and progress on privatisation. Many who have read the earlier review statements will recognise the list. When the same agenda is repeated, the question one must ask is: how much has changed? The Fund’s language of commitment does not answer it. The tranche will arrive. What the government has yet to demonstrate is an economy that grows fast enough to cut poverty and sells more abroad — an issue that cannot be put off much longer.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Moscow disagreement
articles.content: THE fact that a consensus on how to deal with terrorism originating in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan eludes regional states was made clear at the recently held Moscow Format moot. The event was attended by nearly all of Afghanistan’s neighbours, including Pakistan. However, there was no joint statement issued because, in the words of the Russian envoy for Afghanistan, “our Afghan and Pakistani colleagues didn’t see eye to eye”. The Taliban regime had also sent its representatives. The main sticking point was the Taliban’s objection to including Afghanistan in a “terrorist context”. However, as Pakistan’s envoy put it, it was essential to address “the menace of terrorism emanating from Afghan soil”. Russia offered its good offices to help de-escalate matters between Kabul and Islamabad, though it noted that the Moscow Format was not a forum for resolving bilateral disputes. Both the Taliban’s denialism, and Russia’s apparently soft stance towards the Afghan terrorism problem, are unfortunate. Groups that find shelter in Afghanistan under the Taliban threaten the entire region. Thus, all of Afghanistan’s neighbours need to speak with one voice regarding the ‘export’ of terrorism. Russia is the only state that recognises the Taliban regime. Moscow has its own reasons for indulging the Taliban; these include the need to fight IS-K, which is a common enemy of Russia and the Taliban rulers, as well as to check US and Western influence in Afghanistan. But engagement with Kabul must not be allowed to obscure the fact that some of the deadliest terrorist groups in the world find refuge on Afghan soil. Other regional forums, such as the SCO and the ECO, have highlighted the need to address the terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan. China, which has significant economic interests in Afghanistan, has also pointed to this terrorist threat. The UN Security Council, too, has frequently noted that Afghanistan under Taliban rule has once again become a haven for various terrorist groups. Pakistan’s insistence, therefore, that Afghanistan’s terrorism problem be highlighted reflects the reality of the situation. If Kabul addresses the issue sincerely and restrains terrorist groups, it will benefit not only the Afghan people but the entire region.
articles.author: Editorial
